steps.tx: A **Monteggia fracture-dislocation** comprises a fracture of the proximal or middle third of the ulnar shaft accompanied by dislocation of the proximal radiocapitellar joint. Giovanni Monteggia described this lesion in 1814. Because the radius and ulna operate as a closed parallelogram linked by the interosseous membrane, isolated displacement of one forearm bone cannot occur without dislocation of the opposite joint.
steps.say: A Monteggia fracture is a break of the proximal ulna accompanied by dislocation of the radial head. Described by Monteggia in 1814, it illustrates the rule of forearm biomechanics. Because the radius and ulna act as a rigid ring, a displaced fracture of one bone invariably dislocates the other joint.

vis.title: Forearm Ring Biomechanics
rows: Proximal or middle third ulnar shaft

steps.tx: The classic **Bado classification** subdivides Monteggia lesions into four distinct mechanical patterns based on the direction of radial head dislocation. Type I, the most common, features anterior dislocation of the radial head with anteriorly angulated ulnar fracture. Type II features posterior dislocation. Type III involves lateral or anterolateral dislocation with ulnar metaphyseal fracture. Type IV involves fractures of both forearm bones.
steps.say: Bado classified these into four types according to which way the radial head pops out. Type one is most common, with anterior radial head dislocation and anterior ulnar angulation. Type two has posterior dislocation. Type three has lateral dislocation. Type four has fractures of both the radius and ulna with anterior radial head dislocation.

steps.tx: The primary neurological hazard is injury to the **posterior interosseous nerve**, a motor branch of the radial nerve that winds around the radial neck beneath the arcade of Frohse. Stretching over an anteriorly displaced radial head produces wrist drop sparing, because extensor carpi radialis longus remains innervated, but causes complete paralysis of metacarpophalangeal extension (finger drop) without sensory deficit.
steps.say: The posterior interosseous nerve is at high risk as it winds around the radial neck. When the radial head dislocates anteriorly, it stretches this nerve. The patient develops finger drop with loss of thumb extension, but wrist extension is preserved because radial wrist extensors branch higher up. There is zero sensory loss.

left.title: PIN Neuropathy Deficits
points: Inability to extend thumb MCP joint
Preserved sensation over dorsum of hand

right.title: Radial Nerve Trunk Deficits
points: Complete wrist drop with wrist flexion
Sensory numbness over first web space

steps.tx: Radiographic verification requires confirming that the **radiocapitellar line** remains uninterrupted on every projection. On both anteroposterior and lateral elbow radiographs, a line drawn through the longitudinal center of the radial shaft and neck must pass directly through the capitellum. If this line points anywhere away from the capitellum, an unrecognized radial head dislocation is present.
steps.say: Always check the radiocapitellar line on both AP and lateral views. A straight line drawn along the central axis of the radial neck must point directly into the center of the capitellum, no matter how the elbow is rotated. If it misses the capitellum, the radial head is dislocated.

left.title: Normal Radiocapitellar Alignment
points: Line bisects radial neck and shaft

right.title: Dislocation Pitfall
points: Wrist films alone miss elbow joint

steps.tx: Definitive management in adults necessitates anatomic **rigid plate fixation** of the fractured ulna using a dynamic compression plate. Anatomical restoration of ulnar length, alignment, and rotation usually achieves spontaneous, concentric reduction of the radial head. If the radial head remains stubbornly dislocated, open exploration of the joint is mandatory to extract an interposed annular ligament or capsule flap.
steps.say: In adults, treat Monteggia fractures with rigid plate and screw fixation of the ulna. Restoring the exact length and rotation of the ulna almost always pops the radial head back into place spontaneously. If it stays out, open the elbow joint immediately to clear out a folded annular ligament.

vis.title: Treatment Principles by Age
rows: Open reduction if annular ligament blocks
Annular ligament reconstruction with fascia lata

quiz.q: Which motor deficit is characteristic of posterior interosseous nerve injury in a Monteggia fracture?
options: Loss of finger metacarpophalangeal extension with spared wrist extension
Complete wrist drop with numbness over the anatomical snuffbox
Weakness of forearm pronation and index finger flexion
Loss of thumb adduction and clawing of the fourth and fifth digits
quiz.explain: PIN palsy spares the extensor carpi radialis longus (branching above the elbow), preserving wrist extension, but paralyses the extensor digitorum, producing finger drop with zero sensory deficit.

quiz.q: Which Bado classification type features posterior dislocation of the radial head?
quiz.explain: Bado Type II is defined by posterior or posterolateral dislocation of the radial head accompanied by posterior angulation of the ulnar shaft fracture.
